Didn't I see this because I am using gcc? What can I do to tell cmake to use clang instead on ubuntu?

Cheers?

CC=clang CXX=clang++

but on this case it is with clang-analyzer (a another clang tools)
you can use also clang-tidy for this

```suggestion:-0+0
	(void)offset;
```

This returned value is never used. Here the compiler (or whatever lint tool) is forcing us to use this value at the end of the function, but maybe `(void)offset` (and keep the function void) is semantically more correct.

Moreover, the lint function could complain that we don't use the return value, so this is possibly another reason to do something like `(void)offset` if it works.

Returning the offset here is misleading, because the parent function is using the packet size, not the count of decoded bytes, to advance in the dissection. This is useful for example to skip over unknown fields (or even to recover from buggy dissection). The return value you suggest **MUST NOT** (in the sense of RFC2119) be used int the calling function. (The parent COULD compare both values and output an expert info, but I'm not sure this is relevent).

Leaving out the final `offset += 4;` is also not so good, because it acts as documentation, and if there are missing fields someone wants to complete later (or find bugs by reading the code), it's better to keep them in my opinion.
it is why i return the value (for avoid to remove all offset +=... of each switch case...
Does `(void)offset;` solve the warning?
We try to avoid this...
I agree with @Jerome-PS here.

`(void)offset` is a straightforward way of telling the linter to shut up. This is correct because the warning is not useful (and IMO actively detrimental in many cases). Using the wrong function semantics is not a better fix than `(void)offset`.
check the return value, with a expert info should the better idea ;)
This looks OK. Also I don't think it breaks anything in the following changes that I still have to commit.
there is an reason to declare function ?

If you mean using a function as opposed to inlining the code, it is better to have a function because the same code is called from several places depending on the key exchange algorithm used (for example I add Diffie-Hellman in !6030 )

If you mean "is declaration necessary before definition?", then I don't know, it depends on the declaration order and the coding rules which may make declaration mandatory.

Yes it is always good to have more detailed error output.

What is the difference between g_debug and ws_debug and which one should be used?
Good question @jvalverde ?

From my experience today, I had a crash (null pointer dereferencing) just after a ws_debug(...) and it did not get printed. But I re-ran the code by adding a g_debug(...) and I saw its output, so if I'm not mistaken, I would tend to prefer g_debug, because it is easier to use when debugging crashes.

We use wsutil/wslog.h. It was created to fix some perceived deficiencies in GLib logging and some other general improvements but otherwise they are similar. That's what should be used. Having to manage a mix of two different logging systems is not a good outcome.

Actually I had a closer look, and I don't see any output of ws_debug(...) calls. What could I be doing wrong?  
I use the command line `env G_MESSAGES_DEBUG=all wireshark`, which allows me to see g_debug(...) output.  
I also added `#define WS_LOG_DOMAIN "ssh"` in packet-ssh.c
Sorry if it's a RTFM question.

Yes, it is. :smile: No problem.

The equivalent wslog usage would be `env WIRESHARK_LOG_LEVEL=debug wireshark`. By default all domains are shown. If you wanted you could filter to display only the `ssh` domain.

https://wiki.wireshark.org/Development/Tips#printing-to-a-console
For temporary printouts it could be more convenient to use `WS_DEBUG_HERE()` (not documented). It's always active so it must not be committed to the master branch.

Should this declaration be moved inside the `if` block on line 1971?
```suggestion:-0+0
```
We can...
Are there any guidelines with regards to this point in the coding rules?
no guideline for this
